title: Christ and Lord (CCC 436–451)
hook: Christ means anointed; Lord was the name for God

segments.voice: Yesterday, body and soul: dust, then breath, and the soul as the form of the body. Your line was one person. Did the glass of water and the minute of quiet happen? Day one thousand seventy-three.

Is Christ a last name? On a form it would look like one. First name, Jesus. Last name, Christ. Easy to hear it that way. But Christ isn't a surname at all. It's a title, a claim about who he is and what he was sent to do. And the word that so often sits beside it, Lord, is a title too, with a history of its own. Today's word is the first of the two.
screen: `NOT A LAST NAME.` → `A TITLE, AND A CLAIM.` → `LORD: A TITLE TOO.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says it plainly. The word Christ comes from the Greek translation of the Hebrew Messiah, and it means anointed. In Israel, it explains, those set apart for a mission from God were anointed in his name: kings, priests, and now and then a prophet. Oil poured on the head meant this person now belongs to a task. And the Catechism says Jesus fulfilled all of it, as king, priest and prophet at once. There's a scene where the title lands. Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is, and then asks them directly: "But whom do you say that I am?" Peter answers, in the Douay-Rheims, "Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God." The Catechism adds a careful detail. Jesus accepted the title, but with reserve, because it could easily be heard in a political way, a messiah with an army. He kept turning it toward the cross, toward a Son of Man who came to give his life. Then the second title. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Catechism says, God's own holy name, the one not spoken aloud, was rendered by the word Lord. So Lord became an ordinary way of naming God. When the New Testament calls Jesus Lord, it's using that same word. Paul writes that no one can say the Lord Jesus except by the Holy Spirit. And the Catechism draws one more line from it: a Christian, calling Jesus Lord, refuses to hand absolute power over their freedom to any earthly ruler. Two words, then. Christ: anointed for a mission. Lord: the name once kept for God.
screen: `CHRIST: THE GREEK FOR MESSIAH.` · `ANOINTED: KING, PRIEST, PROPHET.` · `ACCEPTED, BUT WITH RESERVE.` · `LORD: THE NAME KEPT FOR GOD.` · then, large: `THOU ART CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Let your hands rest open, palms up, the way a person might hold them to be anointed. If you pray, you can say the words Paul writes about: Jesus is Lord. Say them slowly, once or a few times, and let the breath carry them. If you don't pray, ask a quieter question instead: what has the final say in my day? A phone, a fear, a boss, a hope? Name it, without judging it, and sit with that. The bell holds the time.
Christ. From the Greek for the Hebrew Messiah: the anointed one, set apart by God for a mission, king, priest and prophet. Today's word.
Your line: anointed. Today, when you hear the name Jesus Christ, in a church, a song, or someone's swearing, hear the second word as a title: anointed. Day one thousand seventy-three.

howItsDone: Catholics name Jesus as Christ and Lord in the Creed at Mass and in the prayers of the liturgy, which often end "through Christ our Lord."

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Matthew 16:15 and 16:16.
Etymology (Christ from the Greek for Messiah, meaning 'anointed') and the Lord/Kyrios note are as CCC 436 and 446 state them; CCC paraphrased, not quoted.
CCC 436 says those anointed were kings, priests and 'in rare instances' prophets; rendered 'now and then a prophet'.
CCC 439–440 (accepted with reserve, political sense) and CCC 450 (refusing absolute submission to earthly power) paraphrased.
Practice: 'the words Paul writes about' rests on 1 Cor 12:3.
Original game: Χριστός with stress on the final syllable.
